item.title: Aberrant one-carbon metabolism and ancestral genetics underlie edematous severe acute malnutrition
item.dc:creator: Natasha C. Lie
Yixing Han
Qing Li
Aarti Jajoo
Jared Redmond
Aparna Haldipur
Solome Zewdu
Emilyn Banfield
item.description:
Authors: Natasha C. Lie, Yixing Han, Qing Li, Aarti Jajoo, Jared Redmond, Aparna Haldipur, Solome Zewdu, Emilyn Banfield, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10798
Abstract: Abstract Edematous severe childhood malnutrition is distinct from the non-edematous form of malnutrition and remains a major cause of under-five mortality. Its etiology remains unclear, although aberrant one-carbon metabolism has emerged as a potential contributor. Here, we assess genetic variants at loci known to influence one-carbon metabolism, and determine their association with edematous malnutrition in Jamaica and Malawi. Six loci show evidence of association, including four related to homocysteine and folate metabolism - AHCYL1 , PRICKLE2 , GABBR2 , and PLD2 , with SNPs at the latter three also having direct effects on homocysteine-related metabolites in Mendelian Randomization. Collectively, one-carbon metabolism-related variants were significantly associated with edematous malnutrition (z = 3.2), with population differences linked to a shared East African genetic ancestry and distinct signatures of selection. These findings strengthen evidence implicating aberrant one-carbon metabolism in edematous malnutrition and highlight the utility of cell-free DNA, intra-continental admixture, and population genetics for mapping disease risk.

item.title: Tissue composition shapes differential skeletal integration strategies during axolotl limb regeneration
item.dc:creator: Rita Aires
Sean D. Keeley
Kerstin Brandt
Mário Carreira
Doğa Berşan Güneş
Yağız Savcı
Pedro Capucho
Ulrike Anne Friedrich
item.description:
Authors: Rita Aires, Sean D. Keeley, Kerstin Brandt, Mário Carreira, Doğa Berşan Güneş, Yağız Savcı, Pedro Capucho, Ulrike Anne Friedrich, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10826
Abstract: Abstract Limb regeneration requires rebuilding the missing structures and integrating them with stump tissues. Osteoclast-mediated tissue resorption is essential for skeletal integration during regeneration. However, it is unknown if skeletal tissue composition impacts its resorption and, if so, how it is regulated. Here, we show that osteoclast-mediated skeletal resorption is activated in amputations damaging the diaphysis, but not the epiphysis, of skeletal elements. We found that amputations in the calcified diaphysis trigger the sustained expression of RANKL and the chemokine Loc483 , and that the latter is sufficient to induce osteoclast presence in non-resorbing amputations. Finally, our data suggests that the transcriptomic profile of the apical epithelial cap is impacted by the tissues injured by the amputation. Overall, our work reveals that tissue composition at the amputation plane shapes adaptations of the regenerative program, which ultimately contribute to the near-seamless tissue integration of the regenerating axolotl limb regardless of the amputation position.

item.title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts
item.dc:creator: Angus M. O’Ferrall
David Lally
Peter Makaula
Gladys Namacha
Joseph M. Lewis
Patrick Musicha
Richard N. Goodman
Ellie Allman
item.description:
Authors: Angus M. O’Ferrall, David Lally, Peter Makaula, Gladys Namacha, Joseph M. Lewis, Patrick Musicha, Richard N. Goodman, Ellie Allman, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023–24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Colonisation prevalence rose from 34.1% (95% CI: 27.8–41.0) to 54.2% (95% CI: 46.0–62.3) over one year. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission.

item.title: Genome-reduced Aridivitia evolved predation to thrive in Earth’s oligotrophic depths
item.dc:creator: Xiaonan Wan
Wenlu Feng
Yang Zhang
Tom A. Williams
Gergely J. Szöllősi
Hongyu Dang
Xuejun Yan
James M. Tiedje
item.description:
Authors: Xiaonan Wan, Wenlu Feng, Yang Zhang, Tom A. Williams, Gergely J. Szöllősi, Hongyu Dang, Xuejun Yan, James M. Tiedje, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Deep soils represent one of Earth’s largest yet most enigmatic microbial habitats, where survival strategies under extreme oligotrophy remain poorly understood. Here, we report the Aridivitia group, a globally distributed bacterial lineage enriched in oligotrophic soils and thriving down to 22 m depth across sites in the United States and China. Despite its genome reduction (average size ~2.9 Mb), Aridivitia exhibits high metabolic flexibility in utilizing diverse carbon and energy sources. Cellular, genomic, and metatranscriptomic evidence, including small cell and genome sizes, host-associated metabolism, and the active expression of attachment- and attack-associated surface structures such as Tad pili and pore-forming toxins, indicate a predatory lifestyle in Aridivitia. Ancestral genome reconstruction reveals that Aridivitia originated as free-living mixotrophs, but subsequently lost the ability to fix carbon as they evolved a predatory lifestyle. Collectively, Aridivitia exemplifies a unique evolutionary strategy that reconciles genome reduction with functional versatility, expanding our understanding of microbial adaptation and evolution at the energetic limits of life.

item.title: Lesion penetration predicts tuberculosis treatment shortening through a validated translational tool to de-risk development
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline P. Ernest
Annamarie E. Bustion
Anu Patel
Jansy Sarathy
Firat Kaya
Suyapa Rodriguez
Matthew Zimmerman
Natasha Strydom
item.description:
Authors: Jacqueline P. Ernest, Annamarie E. Bustion, Anu Patel, Jansy Sarathy, Firat Kaya, Suyapa Rodriguez, Matthew Zimmerman, Natasha Strydom, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. Our study generates the most comprehensive database of site-of-disease distribution for 24 drugs and drug candidates in a rabbit model of cavitary TB. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials.

item.title: Integrated multi-omics identifies distinct immune signatures with diagnostic and therapeutic implications in immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis
item.dc:creator: Shi-Long Zhang
Qing-Qing Cai
Jian Zhang
Yuan Liu
Hao Lu
Ye-Rui Zhang
Yu-Chen Xu
Hai-Xiang Peng
item.description:
Authors: Shi-Long Zhang, Qing-Qing Cai, Jian Zhang, Yuan Liu, Hao Lu, Ye-Rui Zhang, Yu-Chen Xu, Hai-Xiang Peng, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-myocarditis) is a rare but frequently fatal immune-related adverse event. A comprehensive understanding of the cellular and molecular determinants driving ICI-myocarditis is essential for improving diagnostic precision and developing targeted interventions. We delineate the immune landscape of ICI-myocarditis via scRNA-seq, flow cytometry, Olink proteomics, and multiplex cytokine profiling. We demonstrate that high levels of baseline ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells are linked to the proinflammatory features of monocytes and in vitro experiments confirm the existence of circulating ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells with a high potential to induce cardiomyocyte apoptosis, supporting their pathogenic potential for cardiomyocyte cytotoxicity. Notably, intercellular crosstalk between these subsets is possibly mediated via the CCL2-CCR2 axis, and its blockade attenuated ICI-induced cardiac injury in vivo. Based on the inflammatory signature in ICI-myocarditis, we develop an 8-protein custom panel with promising performance in distinguishing ICI-myocarditis from other ICIs-treated controls. JAK-STAT pathway activation promotes inflammatory programs in both ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells and monocytes. Furthermore, JAK-STAT inhibition ameliorates cardiac dysfunction and inflammatory infiltration while enhancing the response to anti-PD-1 therapy in mouse models. In summary, this study implicates immune-pathogenic features of ICI-myocarditis and provides a possible basis for future therapies.

item.title: Fever enhances host bacterial defence while limiting mitochondrial damage
item.dc:creator: Yonghan Wu
Elijah Rowe
Albert Siryaporn
Steven P. Gross
item.description:
Authors: Yonghan Wu, Elijah Rowe, Albert Siryaporn, Steven P. Gross
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Infection triggers the fever response, but the response’s effect on antimicrobial peptide (AMP) function remains unknown. We discovered that human AMP LL-37 antibacterial activity is temperature-dependent and were curious as to why. Its temperature dependence is not an accident, as AMPs from other animals with different body temperatures have distinct temperature sensitivities. We find that AMP temperature sensitivities are tuned to animals’ body temperatures, and that for animals able to raise their body temperature, this is used to increase the AMP’s antibacterial efficacy. This effect reflects a balance between optimizing antibacterial killing while minimizing mitochondrial damage. In contrast, cold-blooded animals that are unable to raise their body temperature use a different strategy to avoid mitochondrial damage. Together, this study suggests that fever is beneficial for antimicrobial defense by raising AMP activity towards bacteria while reducing mitochondrial damage when pathogens are absent.

item.title: Orientation tomography of lanthanide-doped nanoprobes by polarization-resolved micro-spectroscopy
item.dc:creator: Lilian Magermans
Marcello Bonetti
Thierry Gacoin
Jongwook Kim
item.description:
Authors: Lilian Magermans, Marcello Bonetti, Thierry Gacoin, Jongwook Kim
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Quantifying three-dimensional (3D) orientation is critical for understanding self-assembly and collective behavior in soft matter and biological systems. Moreover, orientational analysis of anisotropic particles can characterize locally applied forces in fluids. We present a methodology for 3D orientation tomography based on polarization-resolved spectroscopy of lanthanide-doped nanorods exhibiting multiple emission dipoles, enabling 3D orientation measurements from a single viewing angle. We develop a confocal imaging setup optimized for lanthanide luminescence and a theoretical framework to extract both the local director and order parameter in nanorod assemblies. The technique achieves 0.5 μm lateral and 1 μm axial spatial resolution and is demonstrated in dense nematic liquid-crystal assemblies, resolving complex 3D topological structures, and in microfluidic flows, mapping alignment under hydrodynamic shear. This approach provides a versatile platform for quantitative studies of collective orientation, self-assembly mechanics, and alignment induced by external forces, and can be extended to other lanthanide-labeled particles and molecular probes.

item.title: On predictability of slip, rupture geometry, and speed of the 2025 M7.8 Mandalay, Myanmar, earthquake
item.dc:creator: Thomas Ulrich
Xiaoyu Zou
Mathilde Marchandon
Nico Schliwa
Fengzhou Tan
Alice-Agnes Gabriel
Wenyuan Fan
Peter Shearer
item.description:
Authors: Thomas Ulrich, Xiaoyu Zou, Mathilde Marchandon, Nico Schliwa, Fengzhou Tan, Alice-Agnes Gabriel, Wenyuan Fan, Peter Shearer, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10173
Abstract: Abstract The 2025 M 7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.

item.title: Surface carbonation governs olivine reactivity for rapid CO2 mineralization
item.dc:creator: Zihua Shao
Yunfeng Liang
Gyuhwan Jo
Keisuke Nakamura
Takeshi Tsuji
item.description:
Authors: Zihua Shao, Yunfeng Liang, Gyuhwan Jo, Keisuke Nakamura, Takeshi Tsuji
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Ultramafic rocks are a global resource with vast potential for permanent CO 2 mineralization. However, the origin of the striking reactivity difference between Ca- and Mg-bearing olivine remains poorly understood. Here we show that this difference arises not merely from the type of cation, but more fundamentally from how these cations modulate the oxygen reactivity. Nonbridging oxygens serve as the oxygen source for CO 2 surface reactions, which in Ca-olivine reduce the Ca 2+ dissolution barrier by 60% and accelerate ion release by six orders of magnitude. The calculated apparent dissolution rate constants reproduce the experimentally observed complete conversion of Ca-olivine within hours under 1 atm CO 2 . This multiscale framework reveals how surface reactions govern silicate carbonation and provides a predictive basis for modeling and engineering large-scale CO 2 mineralization in both synthetic materials and basaltic reservoirs.

item.title: Replacing anaerobic fermentation with reverse β-oxidation enables growth-coupled evolution for enhanced fatty-alcohol production
item.dc:creator: Bridgie Cawthon
Aidan E. Cowan
Zen Yoshikawa
Kenneth Low
Justin Baerwald
Nawa Raj Baral
Matthew Incha
Jennifer Gin
item.description:
Authors: Bridgie Cawthon, Aidan E. Cowan, Zen Yoshikawa, Kenneth Low, Justin Baerwald, Nawa Raj Baral, Matthew Incha, Jennifer Gin, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Engineering robust fermentation hosts remains a barrier to scalable biomanufacturing. In this work we replace canonical mixed-acid fermentation in Escherichia coli with a redox‑balanced reverse β‑oxidation (rBOX) pathway that produces medium‑chain fatty alcohols and is bioenergetically equivalent to ethanol fermentation. This synthetic fermentation restores anaerobic growth, tightly coupling fitness to product formation and enabling adaptive laboratory evolution that selects for mutations increasing rBOX flux. Evolved strains increase maximum productivity fourfold (110 ± 0.15 mg/L/hr) and titer more than threefold up to 4.0 ± 0.28 g/L compared to the unevolved strain. Proteomic analyses of evolved strains indicate differential expression of enzymes at key metabolic nodes and activation of latent genes with functions overlapping those of rBOX enzymes. These results establish redox-balanced growth coupling as a powerful tool for strain improvement and demonstrate rBOX as a practical synthetic fermentation pathway.

item.title: Evaluating the effects of population mobility on transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic
item.dc:creator: James M. Trauer
David S. Shipman
Matthew Ryan
Alec S. Henderson
Emma S. McBryde
Michael T. Meehan
Romain Ragonnet
item.description:
Authors: James M. Trauer, David S. Shipman, Matthew Ryan, Alec S. Henderson, Emma S. McBryde, Michael T. Meehan, Romain Ragonnet
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Changes to community mobility during the COVID-19 pandemic, together with unprecedented availability of surveillance and mobility data, provide a unique opportunity to quantify the effect of mobility on respiratory infection transmission. We present a renewal model that incorporates epidemiological mechanisms influencing SARS-CoV-2 transmission along with a non-mechanistic scaling process. We compare models with and without mobility using epidemic data from 122 countries and quantify the influence of mobility through reductions in non-mechanistic scaling. In several countries, this non-mechanistic process closely tracks mobility trends and varies substantially less when mobility is incorporated. This is especially evident in Western Europe and North America, but not in several countries of West Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Google and Facebook data produce similar findings, and parks is frequently assigned the lowest weight in the multi-location Google analysis. Mobility trends are strongly aligned with short-term transmission dynamics in many high-income settings, although between-country heterogeneity remains.

item.title: Small viruses reveal bidirectional evolution between HK97-fold viruses and encapsulins via procapsids
item.dc:creator: Abelardo Aguilar
Ingrid Miranda Perez
Omer Nadel
Stephen Nayfach
Luis Ruiz Pestana
Anca M. Segall
Forest L. Rohwer
Simon Roux
item.description:
Authors: Abelardo Aguilar, Ingrid Miranda Perez, Omer Nadel, Stephen Nayfach, Luis Ruiz Pestana, Anca M. Segall, Forest L. Rohwer, Simon Roux, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10571
Abstract: Abstract The HK97-fold is an ancient, conserved protein structure that assembles protein shells, forming the capsids of Duplodnaviria viruses and prokaryotic biochemical compartments called encapsulsins. It has been proposed that encapsulins evolved from HK97-fold viruses. But the higher complexity of viral capsids represents a biophysical paradox in the evolution of HK97-fold protein shells. To resolve this problem, we hypothesize the existence of simpler HK97-fold viral capsids associated with smaller genomes than those of known HK97-fold viruses. Such small viral genomes are searched in environmental metagenomes across public databases, including IMG/M and MGnify. Using hidden Markov models and protein language models, we identify and characterize small viral genomes encoding HK97-fold proteins that exhibit molecular similarities to encapsulins yet lack portal and tail genes. The phylogenetic analyses of HK97-fold proteins reveal independent mixed groups of viruses and encapsulins, and structural analyses identify similarities between encapsulins and procapsids, the immature state of viral capsids. The observations support a bidirectional evolution between encapsulins and HK97-fold viruses enabled by the viral procapsid state. Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

item.title: Universal crystallization kinetics of solution-processed semiconductors
item.dc:creator: Zhitian Ling
Mateusz Brzezinski
Shuanglong Wang
Konstantinos Bidinakis
Lei Gao
Chongyao Li
Xin Zhou
Hai I. Wang
item.description:
Authors: Zhitian Ling, Mateusz Brzezinski, Shuanglong Wang, Konstantinos Bidinakis, Lei Gao, Chongyao Li, Xin Zhou, Hai I. Wang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10785
Abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous crystallization kinetics critically govern the morphology and performance of solution-processed semiconductors, yet morphology control is often achieved through trial-and-error optimization. Quantitative understanding of crystallization is essential for precise morphology control but is limited by the simultaneous occurrence of heterogeneous nucleation and crystal growth. Here, a time-defined induced nucleation strategy has been developed to initiate crystallization at specific stages of solution processing. Systematic variation of nucleation timing reveals three distinct morphological regimes, whose emergence is explained by the concentration-dependent critical cluster radius in bulk, interfacial, and cusp environments. On this basis, a quantitative, dimensionless model is developed for heterogeneous crystallization kinetics across diverse processing conditions. The model demonstrates universality across perovskite and organic semiconductors. In situ studies reveal identical growth kinetics for induced and spontaneous nuclei, validating its generality. The resulting morphology control enables tuning of crystallinity and charge transport in solution-processed transistors.

item.title: The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice
item.dc:creator: Anindya S. Bhattacharjee
Maxime Juventin
Chieko Huber
Burak Unsal
Jean-Rodolphe Renfer
Ivan Rodriguez
Alan Carleton
item.description:
Authors: Anindya S. Bhattacharjee, Maxime Juventin, Chieko Huber, Burak Unsal, Jean-Rodolphe Renfer, Ivan Rodriguez, Alan Carleton
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Working memory (WM) enables the temporary maintenance and manipulation of sensory information to guide behavior, yet the neural circuits supporting this process remain incompletely defined. The claustrum is a highly interconnected brain structure positioned to integrate distributed cortical activity, but its contribution to WM has remained unclear. Here, we combined microendoscopic calcium imaging, chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations in mice performing sensory-guided WM tasks to examine the role of the claustrum in WM. Claustrum neurons exhibited cue-evoked activity that persisted across delay periods and evolved dynamically over time, with population states retaining information about cue identity on single trials. Reducing claustrum excitability during encoding, delay maintenance, or target comparison similarly impaired WM performance across sensory modalities, without affecting sensory processing, motor output, arousal or inhibitory control. Together, these findings reveal an important causal contribution of the claustrum to WM maintenance.

item.title: From ancient practice to modern innovation solving the clay mineral puzzle in brickmaking
item.dc:creator: Sen Wang
Lloyd Gainey
Lihui Liu
Zijun Zeng
Shusheng Xiao
Runliang Zhu
Sara Couperthwaite
Yuantong Gu
item.description:
Authors: Sen Wang, Lloyd Gainey, Lihui Liu, Zijun Zeng, Shusheng Xiao, Runliang Zhu, Sara Couperthwaite, Yuantong Gu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Clay minerals are the most crucial constituents in brickmaking clays, yet the specific role of different clay minerals remain poorly understood due to their natural coexistence and formidable challenges of separation. Here, we design a kaolinite-illite-quartz-feldspar system through a multiple-stage purification strategy, enabling direct evaluation of two of the most critical clay minerals for brick making - kaolinite and illite. Precise tuning the initial clay mineral assemblage yields brick strengths up to 8.5 times the ASTM C62 Grade MW requirement, without upgrading existing production methods. Mineralogical mechanisms responsible for substantial strength enhancement are revealed. Extensive analyses of 60 brick formulations uncovered a breakdown of conventional linear relationships among different brick properties due to the temperature-dependent responses of kaolinite and illite; specific formation pathways of mullite and amorphous phases; and over-firing defects above 1200 °C due to K + -induced fluxing from illite. Notably, a previously unrecognized negative correlation between mullite and brick strength is identified, suggesting a need to reconsider the widely held assumption of mullite as a strengthening phase. This work not only presents insights for optimizing high-strength brick formulations but also opens avenues for investigating the intricate contributions of distinct starting components to key brick performance.

item.title: Evolutionary remodeling of the ventral retina enables aerial vision in the four-eyed fish Anableps anableps
item.dc:creator: Louise Perez
Lina Shi
Alyssa Daspit
Keyla N. Pruett
Carsyn Smith
Anna Prideaux

Patricia N. Schneider
item.description:
Authors: Louise Perez, Lina Shi, Alyssa Daspit, Keyla N. Pruett, Carsyn Smith, Anna Prideaux, Josane F. Sousa, Patricia N. Schneider
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The emergence of evolutionary novelties remains a central challenge in biology, particularly for complex organs such as the vertebrate eye. Here, we use the four-eyed fish Anableps anableps to investigate adaptation to simultaneous aerial and aquatic vision. Single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics reveal that the ventral retina, which processes aerial light, is developmentally expanded and exhibits region-specific opsin expression. Ventral PR1 cones express opn1mw2 rather than the longer-wavelength-sensitive opn1lw paralogs expressed dorsally. Machine-learning predictions indicate that Opn1mw2 is red-shifted relative to Opn1mw1 but remains blue-shifted relative to dorsal Opn1lw pigments. Dorsal-ventral patterning markers further reveal an overrepresentation of ventral retinal identities. Comparative spatial profiling of developing and adult Anableps and killifish indicates dorsal displacement of the retinal boundary, producing a proportionally larger ventral domain. Thus, Anableps evolved aerial vision through developmental expansion of the ventral retina and regional reconfiguration of opsin expression within conserved cone subtypes.

Abstract: Abstract Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition frequently accompanied by psychological comorbidities, such as anxiety and depression. Although current treatments may alleviate some of these symptoms, the intricate pathogenesis of these comorbidities highlights an urgent need for therapeutic strategies with combined anti-inflammatory, barrier-reparative, and microbiota-modulating effects. Herein, we develop a series of nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides (NZEP) by integrating nanozymes with yeast-derived polysaccharides using an insect sclerotization-inspired strategy. Among them, NZEP TA-Ce , with the highest degree of nanozyme-exoskeletonization, is capable of disrupting the inflammatory vicious cycle by inhibiting MAPK and NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling pathways. Oral administration of NZEP TA-Ce in mice enables effective retention and accumulation in inflamed colonic regions, reverses the homeostasis imbalance of intestinal inflammation and promotes intestinal barrier repair. Furthermore, NZEP TA-Ce treatment reverses gut microbiota dysbiosis and optimizes the composition of microbial metabolites, thereby alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms associated with IBD. This study provides a safe and promising therapeutic strategy for the management of IBD patients and their associated psychological comorbidities.

Authors: Fabiola Garcia-Cortizo, Tobias Weber, Hana Nůsková, Daniel Pfaff, Michael Büttner, Angela Wirth, Elisabeth Kliemank, Gernot Poschet, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10784
Abstract: Abstract Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a key regulator of metabolism, controlling flux from glycolysis into the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PDH is often dysregulated in metabolic diseases and cancer. We discover here that in addition to its well characterized regulation by phosphorylation, PDH activity is also regulated via inhibitory oxidation of three cysteines of the DLAT subunit - Cys488, Cys586 and Cys618. Oxidation of these cysteines increases under oxidative stress, and is highly prevalent in mouse and human tissues. This mechanism enables cells to efficiently fight oxidative stress. Under oxidative stress, cells execute a metabolic shift, blocking glycolytic flux into the TCA cycle to shunt glycolytic carbons toward the pentose phosphate pathway. This generates NADPH which cells use to detoxify H 2 O 2 and to reduce oxidized cysteines. We find that DLAT oxidation is required for cells to mount an effective antioxidant response. Mutations preventing DLAT oxidation render PDH resistant to oxidative inhibition, impair NADPH generation, reduce peroxide detoxification, and sensitize cells to oxidative damage and death. DLAT oxidation also drives a Warburg-like metabolic phenotype of increased glucose uptake, elevated lactate secretion, and reduced TCA cycle activity. Thus DLAT oxidation is a redox-sensing mechanism that regulates PDH activity and central carbon metabolism.

Abstract: Abstract Accessible cholesterol, the pool of membrane cholesterol with high chemical activity, regulates vital processes including vertebrate development and pathogen evasion. The mechanisms that govern plasma membrane (PM) cholesterol accessibility are incompletely understood. Using a genome-wide screen we find that acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha (ACC1) loss causes a ~10-fold increase in PM accessible cholesterol in cells and a male mouse model. We demonstrate that reduced fatty acyl-CoA levels, achieved by targeting metabolic enzymes including ACC1, fatty acid synthase (FASN) or acyl-CoA synthetases long chain (ACSL1, 3 and 4), results in the activation of adipose triacylglycerol lipase (ATGL). ATGL activation elevates polyunsaturated diacylglycerols even in triacylglycerol-deficient backgrounds, suggesting that ATGL acts independently of triacylglycerol hydrolysis. These diacylglycerol species are utilized to generate polyunsaturated phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, which raises PM fluidity and cholesterol accessibility. Conversely, ATGL inhibition rigidifies the PM, reducing PM accessible cholesterol. Increased PM fluidity impairs cholesterol transport, triggering SREBP2 activation. This study reveals a surprising link between fatty acid metabolism and cholesterol homeostasis, demonstrating how ATGL-dependent lipid remodeling tunes membrane fluidity to regulate intracellular cholesterol signaling.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10361
Abstract: Abstract Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) require electrolytes with high oxide-ion conductivity at low temperatures (200–400 °C) to reduce costs. Here, we report that Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br exhibits oxide-ion conductivity of 0.01 S cm⁻¹ at 233 °C within the “Norby gap” in dry atmospheres. This performance exceeds that of leading proton conductors, such as BaZr 0.8 Y 0.2 O 2.9 and BaZr 0.4 Ce 0.4 Y 0.1 Yb 0.1 O 2.9 , as well as representative oxide-ion conductors, including yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), LaGaO 3 -based phases (LSGM), and Bi 2 V 0.7 Sb 0.3 O 5.5 . The high conductivity is associated with a layered Sillén structure composed of Bi-containing triple fluorite-like slabs and Br layers, together with oxygen vacancies that enable vacancy-mediated oxide-ion migration. Despite the presence of excess oxide ions, oxide-ion transport predominantly occurs via a vacancy mechanism, as revealed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, static density functional theory calculations, and neutron diffraction analyses. These findings establish a design principle for high-performance oxide-ion conductors based on vacancy-mediated oxide-ion transport in excess-oxygen Bi-containing Sillén oxyhalides.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone inhibitors (RAASi) improve outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but their use is often limited by hyperkalaemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. This double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial evaluated whether sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) enables RAASi up-titration in HFrEF patients with CKD stages 3–5 and serum potassium of 5.0–5.5 mmol/L over 14 weeks. The primary binary outcome was defined as achieving the target dose of RAAS inhibition therapy without reaching hyperkalaemia (serum potassium ≥5.6 mmol/L) over 14 weeks or otherwise. Participants ( n = 112) were randomised 1:1 to receive sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) or placebo. The per-protocol (PP) analyses included 43 out of 53 (81%) in the SZC arm and 53 out of 59 participants (90%) in the placebo arm; the intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses included all 112. At the end of the trial, 24 of 43 participants (56%) in the SZC group achieved the target RAASi dose without developing hyperkalaemia compared with 15 of 53 patients (28%) in the placebo group (PP analysis, p = 0.006, ITT analysis, p = 0.007,). Participants in the SZC group were 3 times more likely to reach the target dose without reaching potassium 5.6 mmol/L (OR = 3.16; 95% CI 1.35–7.39; p = 0.008) than in the placebo group (ITT analysis). No significant differences in adverse events between the two groups were observed. SZC appears to safely support rapid RAASi optimisation in HFrEF patients with CKD. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Wearable devices offer a scalable, objective measurement of physical activity, but most studies reduce these data to a single metric over 7-days. Here, we compare wearable-derived phenotyping approaches to understand their impact on activity-disease associations, analyzing 11 million days of Fitbit data from 29,303 All of Us Research Program participants. We derive four daily activity metrics (step count, peak 1-min cadence, peak 30-min cadence, and heart rate per step) across five time-windows (1-day, 1-week, 1-month, 6-months, 1-year), then run phenome-wide analyses across > 700 incident and >1,400 prevalent disease outcomes. Differences between prevalent and incident associations suggest that activity metrics may act as both early markers of disease and risk factors. These findings highlight how large-scale, longitudinal wearable data can advance understanding of health and disease.

Authors: Shoujie Zhang, Dong Lin, Anwen Yu, Haifeng Qi, Zhongyu Jiang, Xiuhui Zheng, Xiang Feng, Yongning Yang, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Supported two-dimensional noble metal oxides (metallene oxides) hold great promise for heterogeneous catalysis owing to their maximized surface exposure and tunable electronic structures. However, their high surface energy and low oxidation potentials make them intrinsically unstable under reaction conditions. Here, we report an epitaxial strain strategy to stabilize and modulate the electronic structure of supported PtO 2 metallene oxide. By employing rutile TiO 2 and rutile SnO 2 supports with distinct lattice parameters, we achieve epitaxial growth of PtO 2 metallene oxide layers with controlled strain states, where the larger-lattice SnO 2 substrate imposes biaxial tensile strain on PtO 2 . The tensile-strained PtO 2 /SnO 2 exhibits a reconfigured Pt–O electronic environment that simultaneously improves structural resilience and enhances the intrinsic reactivity of PtO 2 , delivering markedly improved methane oxidation performance with a T 90 of 370 °C (versus 434 °C for PtO 2 /TiO 2 and 469 °C for PtO x /Al 2 O 3 ) and <1% conversion loss over 38 h under both dry and wet conditions. Moreover, this epitaxial strain strategy is generalizable to other environmentally relevant oxidation reactions and rutile-type noble metal oxides, establishing tensile strain imposed by epitaxial lattice matching as a general principle for stabilizing atomically thin noble metal oxides while tuning their electronic structure.

item.dc:creator: Bastien Païs
Alexandre Gondran

Florian Simatos
item.description:
Authors: Bastien Païs, Alexandre Gondran, Lorie Hamelin, Florian Simatos
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10736
Abstract: Abstract Aviation decarbonization roadmaps predominantly rely on replacing fossil kerosene with alternative jet fuels, yet the systemic impact of these alternatives on planetary boundaries other than climate change has not been quantified. Here we integrate prospective life-cycle inventories with the planetary boundaries framework to evaluate the absolute impacts of aviation roadmaps as time-dependent trajectories, rather than endpoint snapshots. Across scenarios to 2050, we find that fuel-switch-centered roadmaps do not achieve sustainability, persistently transgress the climate change and biosphere integrity core boundaries, and exert large demands for energy, land, freshwater and CO 2 capture that challenge their feasibility. Slower traffic growth brings aviation closer to its share of the safe operating space in terms of lowering energy demand, but respecting additional planetary boundaries requires air traffic to decline by at least 7.2% yr −1 . Our results show that aligning aviation with Earth’s safe operating space cannot be achieved through fuel substitution alone and requires governance strategies that combine supply-side solutions with explicit demand-side measures.

Abstract: Abstract Electrophysiological signals provide crucial and reliable information for decoding behavioral and cognitive human states. However, existing electrode interfaces are susceptible to artifacts or drift over time, thereby requiring frequent machine-learning model retraining. Here we present an end-to-end design of dry electrodes based on carbon nanotube (CNT) thin films, synthesized by a roll-to-roll floating catalyst chemical vapor deposition process. By balancing structural and electrical properties, we achieved low electrode-skin impedance, high signal fidelity, minimal motion artifacts, high breathability, and biocompatibility, outperforming the gold standard wet electrodes. Abstract: Abstract Impaired adipogenesis contributes to obesity-associated metabolic disorders, in which mitochondrial dysfunction plays an important role. Authors: Patryk Klochowicz, Ahmad F. Kassir, Chandrakanta Parida, Jarosław M. Granda
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Autonomous robotic platforms accelerate chemical discovery by coupling automated experimentation with algorithmic decision-making, but most lack integrated support for chirality and the sequential decision-making required to explore asymmetric reaction spaces with unknown reactivity and stereochemical outcomes. Here, we report a bespoke robotic platform guided by deep reinforcement learning that autonomously navigates a defined asymmetric reaction space by scouting reaction conditions, discovering chiral products, screening catalysts and mapping substrate scope. The structure-agnostic workflow is enabled by a digital twin of asymmetric catalysis, in which control policies are trained before transfer to the laboratory. We validate the approach in chiral phosphoric acid catalysis: over 30 days, the system made more than 3,000 decisions and uncovered four highly enantioselective transformations, including an axially chiral molecule and three allene syntheses, one involving the enantioselective functionalization of a pyrrolopyrrole moiety. Abundant sialidases in deep soils implicate glycoproteins as a key carbon source. Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10741
Abstract: Abstract Magnetic order in van der Waals magnets can strongly influence their lattice dynamics, yet how it affects local and macroscopic manifestations of spin-phonon coupling remains unclear. Optical phonons probe bond-scale exchange modulation and short-range spin correlations, whereas long-wavelength acoustic modes couple to uniform strain fields and are sensitive to renormalization of the macroscopic elastic tensor associated with long-range magnetic order. Experimentally accessing these acoustic excitations in low-dimensional crystals is challenging due to their low energies and the small lateral dimensions of exfoliated samples. Our results show a single Rayleigh surface mode whose phase velocity decreases significantly across the Néel temperature. This anomaly reflects a strong magnetoelastic renormalization of the elastic constants triggered by the onset of antiferromagnetic order. First-principles calculations, combined with continuum finite-element modeling reproduce the Rayleigh-wave dispersion and its magnetic-order–induced shift. The results reveal how microscopic exchange interactions govern the macroscopic elastic response of two-dimensional antiferromagnetic semiconductors, enabling magnetically tunable phononic, magnonic, and strain-mediated spintronic devices.

Abstract: Abstract Sleep consolidates episodic memory through a hippocampus-dependent process in adults. Whether and how sleep supports memory consolidation during early life, when hippocampal function is immature, remains unclear. Abstract: Abstract Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable RNA medicines, yet ionizable-lipid discovery remains largely empirical, particularly when in vitro activity must be translated into functional hepatic delivery in vivo. item.dc:creator: Cheng Jiang

item.description:
Authors: Cheng Jiang, Jinyang Liang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Single-shot fringe projection profilometry (SS-FPP) has been extensively applied to the study of rapid three-dimensional (3D) dynamics in physics, engineering, and biology. Despite these advancements, the imaging capability of time-resolved SS-FPP is still limited by the flexibility and speed of both pattern projection and image acquisition, as well as by the duration of the observation time window. Here, we overcome these constraints by developing chromatically band-limited illumination profilometry (C-BLIP). On the illumination side, C-BLIP projects programmable grayscale fringes at ultrahigh speed by synergizing a digital micromirror device with a user-selectable encoding region of interest and a custom-designed projection lens for chromatically band-limited illumination with incoherent light sources. On the detection side, C-BLIP acquires spatially multiplexed color fringe images, followed by 3D image reconstruction. Using C-BLIP, we demonstrated color 3D imaging of a turbofan blade-projectile collision at 25 thousand frames per second (kfps), as well as intensity 3D imaging of maple samara’s fall aerodynamics at 75 kfps and ultrasound encryption/recovery at 150 kfps. These results highlight C-BLIP’s promise for continuous-streaming, ultrahigh-speed 3D metrology in industrial inspection, bionics, and data security.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are the guardians of translational fidelity. Their complex function is mirrored by an elaborate structure, which includes multiple nested domains. While the evolutionary pressures that promoted the emergence of some domains, such as the editing domain, are clear, the pressures acting on other domains, particularly those at the C-terminus, are not. Here, we combine kinetic analysis, X-ray crystallography, and bioinformatics to unveil the history and evolutionary forces that have shaped isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase (IleRS) domain structure. We find that the traditional classification of IleRSs based on the C-terminal tRNA-recognition domains is incomplete, as it fails to capture features of the synthetic domain. Guided by a crystal structure of the Priestia megaterium IleRS2:tRNA Ile complex, we removed key interactions between IleRS2 and its cognate tRNA and characterised their impact on enzyme activity. We found that D-loop interactions with the IleRS2 C-terminal domains are non-essential in prokaryotes, and their loss can even increase catalytic turnover. Further, we show that the zinc-binding domain of IleRS1 recognises the anticodon less stringently than the canonical C-terminal domain of IleRS2. Our data suggest that C-terminal evolutionary remodelling of IleRSs is an ongoing process with a historical precedent and is consistent with selection for faster aminoacylation rate.

Abstract: Abstract The mitotic chromosome periphery (MCP) is an important chromosome compartment but links to disease remains elusive. Abstract: Abstract Accurate representations of origin-destination (OD) passenger flows on the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. Here we introduce a generative model that treats air mobility as a stochastic process within a sparse maximum-entropy framework, informed by aggregate traffic volumes of individual locations and geographic regions. The model accurately reconstructs both network structure and mobility flows, yielding epidemic spreading trajectories that closely match those obtained using real mobility data. Furthermore, the method can be effectively implemented using open data on flight routes and airport traffic, reducing dependence on proprietary datasets. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for scenario analysis and policy design in global mobility systems.

Abstract: Abstract Thwaites Glacier is a major contributor to Antarctic mass loss and a key source of uncertainty in future sea-level rise. Abstract: Abstract Imagination is a principal human capacity, enabling simulation of sensations and situations for planning, learning, and empathy. These findings suggest that imagination generates distributed pain-like activity, but with separable neural codes for imagined and experienced pain. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Genome stability is essential for cellular viability yet constantly threatened by DNA-damaging agents. Among these, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are particularly harmful and in S/G2 phases are faithfully repaired through homologous recombination (HR). The RAD51 recombinase forms nucleoprotein filaments on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) that performs critical functions in HR. The efficiency of HR depends on precise regulation of RAD51 filament dynamics by accessory factors, including RAD54B, a double-strand DNA-dependent ATPase. Here, using cryogenic electron microscopy, mutagenesis, and biochemical assays, we show that RAD54B stabilizes RAD51–DNA filaments, inhibits RAD51 ATPase activity, and promotes D-loop formation and strand exchange. RAD54B contains two main RAD51-interacting sites and a β-domain that bridges RAD51 protomers, is positioned to contact donor dsDNA, and regulates RAD54B’s ATPase activity. Cellular assays reveal that the RAD51-interacting sites are required for repairing DSBs by HR in human cells. Our findings uncover a modular architecture and mechanistic framework for RAD54B’s critical role in genome maintenance.

Biocompatibility assessments confirm low cytotoxicity, underscoring potential for further development of DB·2TFSI nano-agents. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Subtelomeres are imperfect repeats adjacent to telomeres that are transcriptionally repressed by heterochromatin. Although essential for genome integrity, their repetitive nature has thwarted dissection of local heterochromatin assembly and maintenance mechanisms. By engineering fission yeast strains carrying fluorescent reporters at a single subtelomere, we uncovered distinct subdomains. These subdomains have different silencing requirements: telomere-proximal regions rely on canonical shelterin- or RNAi-dependent nucleation pathways, whereas telomere-distal regions involve nucleosome remodelers, histone chaperones, and boundary-associated factors. We document these epigenetic states using multi-generational live imaging and targeted perturbations. These analyses show that subtelomeric subdomains display position-specific, clonally variable silencing across a spectrum from robust to fragile epigenetic states. Interestingly, structural variants, common in subtelomeric sequences across eukaryotes, dictate local epigenetic stability. These findings reveal that subtelomeres, long recognized for their sequence variability, form a dynamic mosaic of coexisting epigenetic domains. This implies a wide range of gene-repressive regulatory logic at the chromosome ends, from environmental responsiveness to silencing stability.

item.description:
Authors: Robert P. Sosa, Alfredo Jose Florez Ariza, Jeonghoon Kim, Alexander B. Tong, Zhen-Hui Kang, Alicia Li, John Kuriyan, Carlos Bustamante
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract ClpX is a clockwise hexameric helical arrangement that hydrolyzes ATP to unfold proteins and translocate them into the proteolytic chamber. We investigate the central coupler, a three α-helix module conserved among AAA+ ATPases, which is proposed to enable intersubunit communication and mechanochemical coupling. Although fundamental in AAA+ ATPases, the molecular mechanism underlying these processes remains elusive in ClpX. By combining single-molecule optical tweezers, biochemical assays and single-particle cryo-EM we demonstrate that the central coupler, of the second-highest subunit of the ClpX clockwise helical arrangement, positions its Arginine-finger, sensor-I and sensor-II to contact the ATP of the anticlockwise neighbor subunit to trigger its hydrolysis. Then, the central coupler of the highest subunit rapidly couples the ATP hydrolysis with the downward motion of its substrate-translocating loop, enabling fast force generation to swiftly unfold protein substrates while maximizing the thermodynamic efficiency of the motor.

item.description:
Authors: Tristan Cumer, Alexandros Topaloudis, Eleonore Lavanchy, Anne-Lyse Ducrest, Sonia Sarmiento Cabello, Anna Hewett, Paolo Becciu, Céline Simon, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Understanding how wild populations undergo rapid phenotypic evolution requires linking phenotypic change to its underlying genomic architecture over contemporary timescales. Here, we leverage a 30-year study of Swiss barn owls ( Tyto alba ) to examine long-term changes in two melanin-based traits (plumage coloration and spottiness) that have previously been linked to multiple fitness-related traits. We document a consistent temporal shift toward darker and more heavily spotted individuals and show, using whole-genome sequencing of 3,102 individuals, that these traits are controlled by a small number of loci of major effect with partially overlapping architectures. Temporal allele frequency analyses reveal subtle but consistent changes at these loci. By comparing empirical trajectories to simulations, we show that genetic drift alone is insufficient to explain the observed patterns at one major locus, indicating a role for selection. Our results demonstrate how selection acting on a small number of loci can contribute to rapid phenotypic evolution of continuous traits in the wild and highlight the value of long-term genomic and phenotypic monitoring for disentangling evolutionary processes.

item.title: Continuous-time noise mitigation in analogue quantum simulation
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Bressanini
Yue Ma
Michael Hanks
Hyukjoon Kwon
M. S. Kim
item.description:
Authors: Gabriele Bressanini, Yue Ma, Michael Hanks, Hyukjoon Kwon, M. S. Kim
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Analogue quantum simulators offer a promising route to explore quantum many-body dynamics beyond classical reach in the near term. However, their vulnerability to noise limits the accuracy of simulations. Here, we establish a continuous-time framework for mitigating noise in analogue quantum simulation. Our protocol fully preserves the continuous-time nature by avoiding any active control or measurement of the system during the dynamics, while achieving exact noise cancellation. This requires a small number of ancillary qubits, whose interaction with the system, combined with classical post-processing of joint measurement data, is tailored to cancel the effect of noise. Furthermore, the protocol is Hamiltonian-independent and robust to realistic ancilla noise. This work points to a promising direction for achieving high-fidelity analogue quantum simulation in the presence of noise.
